prompt.context: Our client, Vestimenta, is in the business of creating tailor-made clothes for the modern woman with an emphasis on quality and fit. Vestimenta focuses on clothing design, retail, and tailoring. The company's executive team wants to launch in the Bay Area and has hired BCG to evaluate if this is a good idea.
prompt.question: Should Vestimenta launch in the Bay Area, and if so, which retail model should they pursue?

clarifying_info.q: Is Vestimenta a concept or do they have existing stores?
clarifying_info.a: Vestimenta launched in New York City approximately three years ago and has one physical location in Manhattan.
A typical Vestimenta customer is a working woman who's looking for high-quality tailor-made clothing at mid-range prices.

clarifying_info.q: What type of clothing does Vestimenta sell?
clarifying_info.a: Vestimenta sells dresses, blazers, slacks, shirts, skirts, and sweaters.

clarifying_info.q: Does the company have specific goals in mind for this launch?
clarifying_info.a: Vestimenta is looking to get their investment back in two years.
Vestimenta works with many vendors. Their main manufacturers are in Vietnam, Cambodia, and Mexico.

clarifying_info.q: What is the average price point for a Vestimenta item?
clarifying_info.a: An average Vestimenta item is priced at $175-225.

exhibits.title: Vestimenta Brand Context
exhibits.shows: Two photos: a tailor's mannequin with a measuring tape and a professional woman in business attire, conveying the brand's tailor-made positioning for the modern working woman.
exhibits.data: Visual/brand imagery only; no numerical data.

exhibits.title: NYC Store Quarterly Sales Volume by Clothing Type
exhibits.shows: A horizontal bar chart showing quarterly unit volume sold at the NYC store, broken down by clothing category (Tops, Bottoms, Dresses, Blazers). Volumes are per quarter.
exhibits.data: Tops: ~3,000 units/quarter; Bottoms: ~4,000 units/quarter; Dresses: ~2,000 units/quarter; Blazers: ~1,000 units/quarter; Total: ~10,000 units/quarter

exhibits.title: Three Bay Area Retail Model Options
exhibits.shows: A table comparing three retail models (Retail only per location, Try-on Shop + Online, Online only) across revenue, employee costs, marketing expenses, variable costs + other costs, rental costs, and profit growth in Year 2+. Footnotes explain store size, investment, and location count requirements.
exhibits.data: Revenue: NYC / 2*NYC / 2.2*NYC; Employee Costs: 3% of revenue (all three); Marketing Costs: 1% / 2% / 4% of revenue; Variable Costs + Other Costs: 30% / 25% / 20% of revenue; Rental Costs: $7 per sq ft per month (all three); Profit Growth Year 2+: 5% / 30% / 10%. Retail stores: 5,000 sq ft, $6M upfront per store, 3 locations required. Try-on: 1,000 sq ft, $4M per location + $3M warehouse, 1 location. Online only: $6M warehouse, no retail.

framework: Financial Analysis: Estimate revenues and costs for the SF launch (start with NYC store data as baseline)
Market Landscape: Assess Bay Area market size, competitive dynamics, and fit with Vestimenta's target customer
Business Model Evaluation: Compare three entry models (Retail Only, Try-on Shop + Online, Online Only) on profitability and strategic fit
Investment & Payback: Evaluate which option meets the 2-year payback criterion
Risks & Assumptions: Identify key assumptions and risks for the recommended option

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, calculate the annual revenue for the NYC store.
questions.guidance: Candidate should sum the quarterly volumes from Exhibit 2 to get ~10,000 items/quarter, multiply by 4 quarters and by the average price of $200/item. Should proactively ask whether SF product mix and pricing are comparable to NYC.

math.setup: Annual Revenue = quarterly volume * 4 quarters * average price per item
steps: Average price = $200/item (provide if asked; only data available)
math.answer: $8M annual revenue for the NYC store

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 3, calculate the two-year net profit for each of the three Bay Area options and determine which model best meets the client's 2-year investment payback goal.
questions.guidance: Candidate should set up revenue (as a multiple of NYC $8M), then subtract employee + marketing + variable costs (all as % of revenue) and rental costs, to get Year 1 profit. Apply the stated growth rate for Year 2 profit. Sum both years and subtract upfront investment. Strong candidates note that Online Only is most profitable within 2 years, but Try-on + Online has higher growth and becomes most profitable beyond 2 years.

math.setup: For each model: Year 1 Profit = Revenue - (Employee % + Marketing % + Variable %) * Revenue - Rental Cost. Year 2 Profit = Year 1 Profit * (1 + growth rate). 2-year profit = Year 1 + Year 2 - Investment.
steps: Rental costs = $7 * 5,000 sq ft * 12 months * 3 locations = $1.26M ~ $1.3M

Operating costs = (3%+4%+20%) * $17.6M = 27% * $17.6M = ~$4.75M ~ $4.9M (casebook uses marketing 5%+other; note casebook shows .05 for marketing in online only calc = 4% marketing + 1% employee rounding; use 27% total)
math.answer: Within 2 years: Online Only is most profitable (~$20.6M net). However, with 30% Year 2 growth, Try-on + Online becomes most profitable beyond 2 years. Recommended choice depends on time horizon.

brainstorming.prompt: What criteria would you use to evaluate the three Bay Area options? Then, assuming the client goes with Try-on Shop + Online, what are the advantages and disadvantages?

categories.name: Try-on + Online: Advantages
ideas: Reduced retail space (1,000 sq ft vs 5,000) lowers rental costs
Lower investment cost vs retail only ($7M vs $18M)
Smaller inventory needed (custom-tailored, smaller warehouse) reduces cash tied up in inventory
Lower marketing cost than online only
Customers get in-person tailor fit, ensuring clothes fit well and enhancing experience
Captures customer size data enabling repeat purchases with guaranteed fit

categories.name: Try-on + Online: Disadvantages
ideas: Single location captures less foot traffic than 3 retail locations
Longer break-even period than online only (though difference is small)
Still incurs retail costs that online-only model avoids
Assumes customers prefer trying on in store, but free-return shipping from competitors may reduce the appeal of the try-on model

recommendation: Recommend Vestimenta proceed with the Try-on Shop + Online model for the SF Bay Area launch

While Online Only is the most profitable within the 2-year window (~$20.6M vs ~$18.6M net), the Try-on + Online model's 30% Year 2 growth rate makes it the superior long-term choice and it still meets the client's 2-year investment payback criterion
risks: Assumption that the SF market is culturally and economically similar to NYC
Assumption that rental rates in SF remain flat
Risk that SF consumers may not adopt the try-on concept as expected
Multiple cost assumptions (variable costs, growth rates) require validation
Introducing a hybrid model is operationally more complex than a single-channel approach
next_steps: Evaluate actual costs and revenue for existing similar retailers in SF to validate assumptions
Run focus groups, surveys, and consumer research (including factor analysis) to understand SF consumer behavior
Explore long-term lease contracts to lock in favorable rental rates
Assess competitive landscape in SF for tailor-made and premium women's apparel
